title: In the Beginning
subtitle: Genesis 1 to 3, Berean Standard Bible
description: The creation of the world, Eden, and the first human choices.
paragraphs: "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth."
The earth was formless and void. Darkness was over the surface of the deep, and the Spirit of God was hovering over the surface of the waters.
God spoke, and there was light. He separated the light from the darkness and called the light day and the darkness night. Evening came, then morning. The first day was done.
He made the sky and separated the waters above it from the waters below it. The second day was done.

He gathered the waters under the sky into one place, and dry land appeared. He called the dry land earth and the gathered waters seas. The earth brought forth seed-bearing plants and fruit trees, each after its kind. The third day was done.

He set lights in the sky to separate day from night and to mark seasons, days, and years. The greater light ruled the day. The lesser light ruled the night. He made the stars as well. The fourth day was done.
The waters filled with living creatures, and birds flew above the earth. God blessed them and told them to be fruitful and multiply. The fifth day was done.

The earth brought forth livestock, beasts, and every creature that crawls on the ground, each after its kind. Then God made man in His own image, male and female, blessed them, and gave them the earth to fill and rule. He saw all that He had made, and it was very good. The sixth day was done.
On the seventh day God rested from all His work. He blessed the seventh day and sanctified it.
Now the story comes down to the man himself.
The LORD God formed him from the dust of the ground. God breathed the breath of life into his nostrils, and the man became a living being.

The man was placed in a garden God had planted in Eden, in the east. No rain had fallen on the earth yet. Springs welled up from the ground and watered it. In the garden, trees grew that were pleasing to the eye and good for food. In the middle of the garden stood the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. A river flowed out of Eden to water the garden, and from there it divided into four rivers, the Pishon, the Gihon, the Tigris, and the Euphrates.
The man had work there. He was put in the garden to cultivate it and keep it.

He also had a command to learn. God told him he could eat freely from every tree in the garden. From one tree he could not eat. It was the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. In the day he ate from it, he would surely die.
God said, "It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make for him a suitable helper."
Then the animals came to the man.

God had formed every beast of the field and every bird of the air out of the ground, and He brought them to the man to see what he would call each one. The man gave names to all the livestock. He gave names to the birds of the air. He gave names to every beast of the field. Whatever the man called each living creature, that was its name.

Name after name was spoken in that garden. Creature after creature passed in front of him. When the naming was done, the result stood plain in front of him. For Adam no suitable helper had been found.
God caused the man to fall into a deep sleep.
While he slept, God took one of the man's ribs and closed up the place with flesh. From the rib He made a woman. Then God brought her to the man.
The man woke to someone who had not been there before he slept. She was made from him, and she was not another animal he had named. He spoke at once.
"This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called 'woman,' for out of man she was taken."
For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and they will become one flesh. The man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed.
In the garden with them was the serpent. He was more crafty than any beast of the field that the LORD God had made.
The serpent spoke to the woman. His first move was a question.
"Did God really say, 'You must not eat from any tree in the garden?'"

The woman answered what she had been told. They could eat the fruit of the trees of the garden. About the fruit of the tree in the middle of the garden, God had said they must not eat it or touch it, or they would die.
The serpent contradicted God to her face. She would not surely die, he told her. God knew that in the day she ate from it, her eyes would be opened and she would be like God, knowing good and evil.
The woman looked at the tree in front of her. She saw that it was good for food. She saw that it was pleasing to the eyes. She saw that it was desirable for obtaining wisdom.
She took its fruit and ate it. She gave some to her husband, who was with her, and he ate it.
At once their eyes were opened. They knew that they were naked. They sewed fig leaves together and made coverings for themselves.
Then the man and his wife heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden in the breeze of the day. They hid themselves from His presence among the trees of the garden.
God called to the man. "Where are you?"
The man answered from where he was hiding. He had heard God's voice in the garden. He was afraid because he was naked, so he hid himself.
God asked who had told him he was naked. God asked if he had eaten from the tree He commanded him not to eat from.
The man pointed to the woman. The woman whom God gave him, she gave him fruit from the tree, and he ate it.
God asked the woman what she had done.
She said the serpent deceived her, and she ate.

God dealt with them in order. He spoke to the serpent first. Because he had done this, he was cursed above all livestock and every beast of the field. On his belly he would go, and dust he would eat, all the days of his life. God would put enmity between him and the woman, and between his seed and her seed. He would crush the serpent's head, and the serpent would strike his heel.
To the woman, God said He would sharply increase her pain in childbirth. In pain she would bring forth children. Her desire would be for her husband, and he would rule over her.

To Adam, God said the ground was cursed because of him. He had listened to the voice of his wife and eaten from the tree God commanded him not to eat from. Through toil he would eat of the ground all the days of his life. The ground would yield thorns and thistles for him. By the sweat of his brow he would eat his bread, until he returned to the ground from which he was taken. For dust he was, and to dust he would return.
Adam named his wife Eve, because she would be the mother of all the living.
God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife, and He clothed them.

Then Adam learned the last hard fact of that day. God said the man had become like one of Them, knowing good and evil. Now he could not be allowed to reach out his hand, take also from the tree of life, eat, and live forever.

The LORD God banished him from the Garden of Eden to work the ground from which he had been taken. He drove the man out. At the east side of the garden He stationed cherubim and a whirling sword of flame, set there to guard the way to the tree of life.

title: Cain and Abel
subtitle: Genesis 4 to 6, Berean Standard Bible
description: Two brothers, the generations beyond Eden, and a world awaiting Noah.
paragraphs: East of Eden, life went on outside the guarded garden.

Adam and Eve had children. Generations would pass, families would spread across the earth, and the ground God had cursed would have to be worked by hand. But the story slows down first for two brothers, because what happened between them showed how fast trouble had moved from a garden to a field.
The older brother was Cain. The younger was Abel.
Adam had relations with his wife Eve, and she conceived and gave birth to Cain. She said, "With the help of the LORD I have brought forth a man."
Later she gave birth to Cain's brother Abel.
The brothers grew into different work. Abel kept sheep. Cain tilled the soil.
In the course of time, both brothers brought an offering to the LORD. Cain brought some of the fruit of the soil. Abel brought the best portions of the firstborn of his flock.
The LORD looked with favor on Abel and his offering. He had no regard for Cain and his offering.
Cain saw the difference. He became very angry, and his countenance fell.
God spoke to him before he did anything else.

"Why are you angry," said the LORD to Cain, "and why has your countenance fallen? If you do what is right, will you not be accepted? But if you refuse to do what is right, sin is crouching at your door; it desires you, but you must master it."
The warning was in front of Cain, plain and direct. He still called his brother out.
Cain said to his brother Abel, "Let us go out to the field."
While they were in the field, Cain rose up against his brother Abel and killed him.
Abel was dead. Cain stood in a field with no brother beside him, and then God's voice came again.
The LORD said to Cain, "Where is your brother Abel?"
Cain answered, "I do not know! Am I my brother's keeper?"

God knew what the field held. "What have you done?" He said. "The voice of your brother's blood cries out to Me from the ground. Now you are cursed and banished from the ground, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother's blood from your hand. When you till the ground, it will no longer yield its produce to you. You will be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth."
Cain's own work had turned against him. The soil he tilled would not produce for him, and the earth he lived on would not give him a settled place.

Cain said his punishment was greater than he could bear. God had driven him from the face of the earth. He would be hidden from God's face. He would be a fugitive and a wanderer, and whoever found him would kill him.
The LORD answered, "Not so! If anyone slays Cain, then Cain will be avenged sevenfold."
God placed a mark on Cain, so that no one who found him would kill him.
Cain went out from the presence of the LORD. He settled in the land of Nod, east of Eden.

Life kept building in Cain's line. Cain had a son named Enoch, and Cain built a city and named the city after his son. Generations followed. Irad was born to Enoch. Irad was the father of Mehujael. Mehujael was the father of Methusael. Methusael was the father of Lamech.

Lamech married two women, Adah and Zillah. Adah gave birth to Jabal, the father of those who dwell in tents and raise livestock. Jabal's brother Jubal was the father of all who play the harp and flute. Zillah gave birth to Tubal-cain, a forger of every implement of bronze and iron. His sister was Naamah.

Then Lamech spoke to his wives, and his words were a boast about killing. He had slain a man for wounding him, a young man for striking him. If Cain was avenged sevenfold, Lamech said, then Lamech would be avenged seventy-sevenfold.
Adam and Eve had another son. Eve named him Seth, saying, "God has granted me another seed in place of Abel, since Cain killed him."
Seth had a son and called him Enosh. At that time men began to call upon the name of the LORD.

The years ran long in Seth's line. Adam lived 930 years and died. Seth lived 912 years and died. Enosh, Kenan, Mahalalel, and Jared followed, father to son, and each man lived, had other sons and daughters, and died.

One name breaks the pattern when the reader reaches him. Enoch became the father of Methuselah at 65 years old. After that, Enoch walked with God 300 years. His total years were 365. Then the line changes its rhythm. Enoch walked with God, and then he was no more, because God had taken him away.

Methuselah lived 969 years, longer than anyone else in the list, and died. His son Lamech had a son at 182 years old and named him Noah, saying, "May this one comfort us in the labor and toil of our hands caused by the ground that the LORD has cursed."
Noah grew. After Noah was 500 years old, he became the father of Shem, Ham, and Japheth.

By then men had begun to multiply on the face of the earth, and daughters were born to them. The sons of God saw that the daughters of men were beautiful, and they took as wives whomever they chose. The LORD said His Spirit would not contend with man forever, for man is mortal, and his days would be 120 years. The Nephilim were on the earth in those days, and afterward as well. Their children became the mighty men of old, men of renown.

Then the reader is shown what God saw. The wickedness of man was great upon the earth. Every inclination of the thoughts of man's heart was altogether evil all the time. The LORD regretted that He had made man on the earth, and He was grieved in His heart.

God said He would blot out man, whom He had created, from the face of the earth. Man and beast and crawling creature and bird of the air would be blotted out, for God was grieved that He had made them.
The sentence stood over the whole earth. One man stood out inside it.
"Noah, however, found favor in the eyes of the LORD."

title: Noah and the Flood
subtitle: Genesis 6 to 9, Berean Standard Bible
description: Noah, the ark, the flood, the dove, and the covenant marked by the rainbow.
paragraphs: Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD. Now the reader learns what set him apart in the world he lived in.
Noah was a righteous man, blameless in his generation. Noah walked with God. He had three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth.

The earth around him was corrupt in the sight of God, and it was full of violence. God looked upon the earth and saw that it was corrupt, for all living creatures on the earth had corrupted their ways.
Then God spoke to Noah.
He told Noah the end of all living creatures had come before Him, because through them the earth was full of violence. God would destroy both them and the earth.
Noah's work started with measurements.
God told him, "Make for yourself an ark of gopher wood; make rooms in the ark and coat it with pitch inside and out."

The ark was to be 300 cubits long, 50 cubits wide, and 30 cubits high. Noah was to make a roof for it, finish its walls a cubit from the top, place a door in its side, and build lower, middle, and upper decks.
God told him why the ark had to hold so much. God would bring floodwaters upon the earth to destroy every creature under the heavens that had the breath of life. Everything on the earth would perish.

Inside that sentence came a promise Noah had not heard before. God would establish His covenant with Noah. Noah would enter the ark with his sons, his wife, and his sons' wives. He was to bring two of every living creature into the ark, male and female, to keep them alive with him. Two of every kind of bird, animal, and crawling creature would come to him to be kept alive. He was to take every kind of food that is eaten and gather it for himself and for the animals.
Noah did everything precisely as God had commanded him.

Then the LORD spoke again. Noah was to go into the ark, he and all his family, because God had found him righteous in this generation. He was to take seven pairs of every kind of clean animal, a male and its mate, a pair of every kind of unclean animal, and seven pairs of every kind of bird of the air, male and female, to preserve their offspring on the face of all the earth. In seven days God would send rain on the earth for forty days and forty nights, and He would wipe from the face of the earth every living thing He had made.
Noah did all that the LORD had commanded him.

Noah was 600 years old when the floodwaters came upon the earth. He entered the ark with his wife, his sons, and their wives, to escape the waters. The clean and unclean animals, the birds, and everything that crawls along the ground came to Noah and entered the ark two by two, male and female, as God had commanded him. Then the LORD shut him in.

After seven days, the floodwaters came. In the six hundredth year of Noah's life, on the seventeenth day of the second month, all the fountains of the great deep burst forth and the floodgates of the heavens were opened. Rain fell on the earth for forty days and forty nights.

The water did not stop at riverbanks. For forty days the flood kept coming, and the waters rose and lifted the ark high above the earth. The waters surged and rose greatly, and the ark floated on the surface. The waters prevailed until all the high mountains under all the heavens were covered. The waters rose and covered the mountaintops to a depth of fifteen cubits.

Every living thing that moved on the earth perished: birds, livestock, animals, every creature that swarms on the earth, and all mankind. Everything on dry land that had the breath of life in its nostrils died. Every living thing on the face of the earth was blotted out. Only Noah remained, and those with him in the ark.
The waters prevailed on the earth for 150 days.
Noah did not learn the state of the world all at once. He learned it in stages, the way a man sealed inside an ark would have to learn it.

But God remembered Noah, and all the animals and livestock that were with him in the ark. God sent a wind over the earth, and the waters began to subside. The springs of the deep and the floodgates of the heavens were closed, and the rain from the sky was restrained. The waters receded steadily from the earth. After 150 days the waters had gone down.

On the seventeenth day of the seventh month, the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat. The waters continued to recede until the tenth month. On the first day of the tenth month, the tops of the mountains became visible.

After forty days Noah opened the window he had made in the ark and sent out a raven. The raven kept flying back and forth until the waters had dried up from the earth. The raven told him nothing clear.

Then Noah sent out a dove to see if the waters had receded from the surface of the ground. The dove found no place to rest her foot. She returned to him in the ark, because the waters were still covering the surface of all the earth. Noah reached out his hand and brought her back inside.
He waited seven more days and sent the dove out again. This time she came back in the evening. In her beak was a freshly plucked olive leaf. Noah knew that the waters had receded from the earth.
He waited seven more days and sent the dove out again. This time she did not return to him.

In Noah's six hundred and first year, on the first day of the first month, the waters had dried up from the earth. Noah removed the covering from the ark and saw that the surface of the ground was dry. By the twenty-seventh day of the second month, the earth was fully dry.

Then God told Noah to come out of the ark, with his wife, his sons, and their wives. He was to bring out all the living creatures with him, so they could spread out over the earth and be fruitful and multiply on it.
Noah came out. His sons, his wife, and his sons' wives came out with him. Every living creature, every creeping thing, and every bird came out of the ark, kind by kind.
Noah built an altar to the LORD. Taking from every kind of clean animal and clean bird, he offered burnt offerings on the altar.

The LORD smelled the pleasing aroma and said in His heart that He would never again curse the ground because of man, even though every inclination of man's heart is evil from his youth. He would never again destroy all living creatures as He had done. As long as the earth endures, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night would never cease.

God blessed Noah and his sons. He told them to be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth. The fear and dread of them would fall on every living creature, and all creatures were delivered into their hand. Everything that lives and moves would be food for them, just as God had given them the green plants. They must not eat meat with its lifeblood still in it. God would require an accounting from anyone who took the life of his fellow man, for in the image of God, God had made mankind.

Then Noah heard the word covenant spoken over his whole family, and over every living creature that had come out of the ark with him. God established His covenant with Noah, his descendants after him, and every living creature. "Never again will all life be cut off by the waters of a flood; never again will there be a flood to destroy the earth."

God gave a sign for the covenant. "I have set My rainbow in the clouds, and it will be a sign of the covenant between Me and the earth." Whenever clouds formed over the earth and the rainbow appeared in the clouds, God would remember the covenant between Him and every living creature. The waters would never again become a flood to destroy all life.
Noah's three sons were the men from whom the whole earth was populated. Shem, Ham, and Japheth came out of the ark, and Ham was the father of Canaan.

After the flood, Noah, a man of the soil, planted a vineyard. When he drank some of its wine, he became drunk and uncovered himself inside his tent. Ham, the father of Canaan, saw his father's nakedness and told his two brothers outside.

Shem and Japheth took a garment and placed it across their shoulders. Walking backward, they covered their father's nakedness. Their faces were turned away, so they did not see their father's nakedness.

When Noah awoke from his drunkenness, he learned what his youngest son had done to him. He cursed Canaan, saying Canaan would be a servant of servants to his brothers. He blessed the LORD, the God of Shem, and said Canaan would be the servant of Shem. He asked God to expand the territory of Japheth, that Japheth would dwell in the tents of Shem, and that Canaan would be his servant.
After the flood Noah lived 350 years. He lived a total of 950 years, and then he died.
The earth had a population again, and it all traced back to three brothers who had walked out of the ark.
